title: SI units, metric prefixes and measurement tools
blurb: Name the SI base units, convert between metric prefixes in the right direction, and pick the right tool for every lab measurement.
question: A pre-nursing student must record the mass of a tablet in grams, measure 18.0 mL of saline as accurately as possible and find the volume of an irregular pebble. Which instrument does each job, and what units go in the lab notebook?

teach.h: One measuring language for all science
teach.body: Formally, the International System of Units (SI) is a set of seven base units from which every other scientific unit is built. In plain English: scientists everywhere agree on the same few starting units (meter, kilogram, second, kelvin and three more) and make bigger or smaller versions with prefixes that move in powers of 10. Learn the base units, the prefixes and the right tool for each quantity, and most S.4.1 items become quick.

head: Quantity
Unit
Symbol
teach.caption: Two favorite exam traps live here: the base unit of mass is the kilogram (not the gram), and of temperature the kelvin (not the degree Celsius).

teach.body: Other units are built from the base units. Volume is usually given in liters (L): 1 L = 1,000 mL = 1 dm³, and 1 mL = 1 cm³ (the 'cc' on a syringe). Density is g/mL or g/cm³. Force is measured in newtons (N), energy in joules (J), and pressure in pascals (Pa), with 1 atm = 101.3 kPa = 760 mmHg. A food Calorie is 1 kilocalorie.

teach.h: The prefix ladder, largest to smallest

head: Prefix
Symbol
Factor
teach.caption: 1 g = 1,000 mg and 1 mg = 1,000 mcg. Between milli and micro the jump is a factor of 1,000, not 10.

items: Larger unit to smaller unit: multiply (move the decimal point right). 2.5 kg = 2,500 g.
Smaller unit to larger unit: divide (move the decimal point left). 750 mg = 0.75 g.
Count the steps on the ladder: each step between kilo and milli is a factor of 10.
Sense-check: there should be MORE of a smaller unit. 0.045 m is 45 mm, not 0.045 mm.

teach.h: The right tool for the job
head: Tool
Measures
Tip
teach.caption: Also know: thermometer (temperature), stopwatch (time), sphygmomanometer (blood pressure), barometer (air pressure), pH meter (acidity). A Petri dish or Bunsen burner measures nothing.

rows.label: What it is
values: Force of gravity on the mass

teach.caption: Weight = mass x g, where g is about 9.8 m/s² on Earth. Move an object anywhere and its mass stays the same.

teach.body: Aaliyah, applying to an ADN program, has three tasks. She weighs a tablet on an electronic balance: 0.325 g, which is 325 mg (larger to smaller unit, multiply by 1,000). She measures 18.0 mL of saline in a 25 mL graduated cylinder, reading the bottom of the meniscus at eye level, not with a beaker. For a pebble she fills a cylinder to 30.0 mL, drops it in and reads 34.5 mL: the pebble's volume is 4.5 mL, or 4.5 cm³.

teach.text: Classic swaps: a BALANCE measures mass and a SPRING SCALE measures weight (not the reverse). A beaker gives only a rough volume. Microscope magnification is MULTIPLIED, not added: a 10x eyepiece with a 40x objective gives 400x, not 50x. And mg to g means DIVIDE by 1,000.

items: SI base units: meter, kilogram, second, kelvin, mole, ampere, candela.
Larger to smaller unit: multiply. Smaller to larger: divide.
Graduated cylinder for liquid volume (bottom of meniscus, eye level); beakers are rough only.
Balance = mass; spring scale = weight. Mass never changes with location.
Total magnification = ocular x objective; coarse focus on low power, fine focus on high power.

summary: You can now name the SI base units, move up and down the metric prefix ladder in the right direction, and choose the right instrument for length, mass, weight and volume. You can also find the volume of an irregular solid by displacement and calculate a microscope's total magnification.

A.q: Which list contains ONLY SI base units?
A.why: The SI base units for length, mass, time and temperature are the meter, kilogram, second and kelvin.

whyNot.0: The base unit of mass is the kilogram. The gram is a prefixed fraction of it.
whyNot.2: The liter is a derived/accepted unit of volume (1 L = 1 dm³), not a base unit.
whyNot.3: The SI base unit of temperature is the kelvin. The degree Celsius is a related scale, not the base unit.

A.q: A prenatal vitamin label lists 0.4 mg of folic acid per tablet. How many micrograms (mcg) is this?
A.why: 1 mg = 1,000 mcg. Going from a larger unit to a smaller unit, multiply: 0.4 x 1,000 = 400 mcg.

whyNot.0: This multiplies by 10, as if milli and micro were one ladder step apart. They are a factor of 1,000 apart.
whyNot.1: This multiplies by 100. The milli-to-micro factor is 1,000.
whyNot.3: This multiplies by 10,000, one decimal place too far.

A.q: A student must measure 37.5 mL of saline as accurately as possible. Which item on the bench should she use?
A.why: A graduated cylinder is marked for measuring liquid volume fairly precisely, and a 50 mL cylinder covers 37.5 mL.

whyNot.0: Beakers are for holding, mixing and heating. Their markings give only a rough volume.
whyNot.2: An Erlenmeyer flask, like a beaker, gives only a rough volume.
whyNot.3: A volumetric flask is very precise but measures one fixed volume, here 50.00 mL, not 37.5 mL.

B.q: An astronaut has a mass of 72 kg on Earth. Which statement describes her on the Moon?
options: Mass 72 kg; weight about 1/6 of Earth's
Mass 12 kg; weight about 1/6 of Earth's
Mass 72 kg; weight the same as on Earth
Mass 12 kg; weight the same as on Earth
B.why: Mass is the amount of matter and does not change with location. Weight is the force of gravity on that mass, and Moon gravity is about 1/6 of Earth's.

whyNot.1: Dividing the mass by 6 confuses mass with weight. Her amount of matter is unchanged.
whyNot.2: Weight depends on gravity, so it falls on the Moon.
whyNot.3: This reverses the two ideas: mass stays the same and weight changes.

B.q: Which technique gives the correct reading of water in a graduated cylinder?
options: Eye level, at the top edge of the meniscus
From above, at the bottom of the meniscus
Eye level, at the bottom of the meniscus
From above, at the top edge of the meniscus
B.why: Water curves down in the middle, so read the bottom of the meniscus, with your eye level with the liquid surface to avoid parallax.

whyNot.0: Eye level is right, but the top edge (where water climbs the glass) overstates the volume.
whyNot.1: The bottom of the meniscus is right, but viewing from above causes parallax error.
whyNot.3: Both the viewing angle and the reading point are wrong here.

B.q: A student views cheek cells with a 10x eyepiece and switches from the 10x to the 40x objective lens. How does the total magnification change?
B.why: Total magnification = ocular x objective: 10 x 10 = 100x, then 10 x 40 = 400x.

whyNot.0: This adds the two lenses (10 + 10, 10 + 40). Magnifications multiply.
whyNot.1: This ignores the eyepiece, which also magnifies 10x.
whyNot.2: This multiplies for the first lens but then adds 40. Each total is ocular x objective.

C.q: A cylinder holds 35.0 mL of water. After an irregular stone is lowered in, the level reads 47.5 mL. What is the stone's volume?
C.why: Displacement: volume = final level - initial level = 47.5 - 35.0 = 12.5 mL, and 1 mL = 1 cm³, so 12.5 cm³.

whyNot.0: 47.5 mL is the water plus the stone. Subtract the starting 35.0 mL.
whyNot.2: This adds the two readings instead of subtracting them.
whyNot.3: 1 mL equals 1 cm³, so no factor of 1,000 is needed.

C.q: Which pairing of a quantity with its instrument is CORRECT?
C.why: A spring scale measures a force, so it gives weight in newtons. A balance compares masses.

whyNot.1: A spring scale measures weight (a force). Mass in grams is read on a balance.
whyNot.2: A triple-beam balance measures mass, not weight.
whyNot.3: An Erlenmeyer flask gives only a rough volume. Use a graduated cylinder, pipette, burette or volumetric flask.

C.q: A wound is measured at 0.045 m long. Which value is equal to this length?
C.why: 1 m = 1,000 mm, and meters to millimeters is larger to smaller, so multiply: 0.045 x 1,000 = 45 mm (which is also 4.5 cm).

whyNot.0: This multiplies by 100, the meter-to-centimeter factor, and then labels the result in millimeters.
whyNot.1: 0.045 m is 4.5 cm. 45 cm would be 0.45 m.
whyNot.2: This multiplies by 10,000, one place too far.

reteach.title: Metric units work like money
reteach.question: A dollar splits into 10 dimes or 100 cents. How does that make deci, centi and the rest of the metric ladder easy?

blocks.h: Dimes and cents are deci and centi
blocks.body: A dollar is the base unit. A dime is a tenth of a dollar (deci = 0.1), and a cent is a hundredth (centi = 0.01). If you swap dollars for cents you get MORE of them, so you multiply: $3.50 is 350 cents. Going back to dollars you divide. Metric units behave exactly the same way, with kilo (a 'thousand-dollar bill') above and milli (a tenth of a cent) below.

blocks.caption: Each move to a smaller unit gives a bigger number. Going up the ladder, divide.

blocks.text: If your answer has FEWER of a smaller unit (0.4 mg turning into 0.0004 mcg), you went the wrong way. Smaller units always mean bigger numbers.

explain.body: Seven base units: meter (length), kilogram (mass), second (time), kelvin (temperature), mole (amount), ampere (current), candela (light). Liters, newtons and joules are derived units built from these.

items.label: mass: the only base unit with a prefix

test.q: Which of these is an SI base unit?
test.why: The kelvin is the SI base unit of temperature.

whyNot.0: The liter is a derived/accepted unit of volume.
whyNot.1: The base unit of mass is the kilogram, not the gram.
whyNot.3: Celsius is a temperature scale in everyday use, but the SI base unit is the kelvin.

explain.body: Kilo, hecto, deka, base, deci, centi, milli: each step is a factor of 10. Larger unit to smaller unit, multiply; smaller to larger, divide. Milli to micro is a jump of 1,000.

test.q: A specimen has a mass of 3,750 g. What is its mass in kilograms?
test.why: Grams to kilograms is smaller to larger, so divide by 1,000: 3,750 ÷ 1,000 = 3.75 kg.

whyNot.0: This divides by 10,000, one place too far.
whyNot.1: This divides by 100, as if kilo were two steps above the base unit.
whyNot.3: This divides by 10. Kilo is three steps (a factor of 1,000) above the gram.

explain.body: For accurate liquid volume use a graduated cylinder, pipette, burette or volumetric flask. Beakers and Erlenmeyer flasks are for holding, mixing and heating: rough volume only. Read a cylinder at eye level at the bottom of the meniscus.

test.q: A titration needs small volumes of acid added drop by drop and read precisely. Which piece of glassware is designed for this?
test.why: A burette delivers small, precisely measured volumes and is the standard titration tool.

whyNot.1: A beaker gives only a rough volume.
whyNot.2: The Erlenmeyer flask usually holds the solution being titrated; it does not measure the added volume precisely.
whyNot.3: A graduated cylinder is fairly precise but cannot dispense controlled drops the way a burette can.

explain.body: A balance measures mass (kg or g), which never changes with location. A spring scale measures weight, a force in newtons that depends on gravity. A microscope's total magnification is ocular x objective.

test.q: A triple-beam balance is used to measure which quantity?
test.why: A balance compares an object's mass against known masses, giving mass in grams.

whyNot.0: Weight in newtons is measured with a spring scale.
whyNot.2: Density needs a mass AND a volume measurement; a balance alone gives only mass.
whyNot.3: The pascal is a unit of pressure, not force, and a balance measures neither.
